## Agenda Implications

The agenda for the May 5 city council meeting is not yet available.

For this meeting, what is certain is that the council is scheduled to vote on the school budget's total bottom-line figure — the legally constrained role confirmed on April 14. The FY27 budget already passed the school board 4-2 on April 7, so the council's vote is the next formal step in the approval chain ahead of the June 9 referendum.

Jaylen should expect that the council discussion, like the board's, will operate at the total-dollar level rather than the program level. No councilor has the legal authority to name, protect, or cut a specific SPHS program through this vote. Public comment at city council meetings has no disclosed equivalent to the board's 75-minute cap, so testifying is an option — but testimony about specific programs will land in a body that cannot act on it at that level of detail.

What matters for Jaylen: this meeting is a signal checkpoint, not a decision point for anything he cares about by name. The vote matters for the referendum context, but the council cannot restore the art position, protect theater staffing, or reverse the co-curricular stipend reduction. That said, what councilors say during deliberation — how they frame their votes, whether anyone acknowledges SPHS programs by name, whether anyone raises the $360,000 banking decision or the FY28 warning — tells Jaylen how much the city's elected officials even know about what's happening inside his school building.

- Whether Councilor Walker — who has consistently named compound disinvestment across schools, library, Mahoney, and housing — brings any of those threads into the school budget discussion. She is the councilor most likely to connect dots Jaylen cares about.
